Empirical Research Plan: The Causal Effect of Attending a Higher-Quality Secondary School in Trinidad & Tobago

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD)

Why FRD fits

• Assignment to secondary schools is rule-based: each school has an explicit SEA score cutoff that varies by year and cohort.  
• Students just above a school’s cutoff face a discrete upward jump in the probability of attending that higher-quality school, while those just below attend a lower-quality alternative.  
• Treatment take-up is imperfect (e.g., students who live far away may decline a place), so the discontinuity is in the first stage, not deterministically in treatment status ⇒ fuzzy, not sharp, RDD.  
• The FRD delivers a local average treatment effect (LATE) for students whose school assignment is margin-determined by the cutoff—exactly the policy-relevant group.

Alternative strategies (DID, panel IV) are unnecessary because the assignment rule already gives a valid quasi-experiment with minimal functional-form assumptions.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
  T_i = 1 if student i actually attends a “high-quality” school (top-tier or above-median SEA cutoff), 0 otherwise.

Control group
  Students with SEA scores just below the relevant school cutoff who therefore attend the next-best (lower quality) institution.

Running variable
  R_i = SEA standardized score (centered at 0 for each school-cohort cutoff).

Cutoff
  c_s,y = official minimum score for admission to school s in cohort y.  
  For estimation we stack multiple (s,y) cells and re-center scores:  
      running_it = SEA_it – c_s(it),y(it).

Treatment timing
  Single, immediate “event”: admission into secondary school at age ≈11; outcomes measured in later years (Form 3 scores, CSEC results, tertiary enrollment, etc.).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in SEA score at the cutoff.  
     Plausible: SEA is a high-stakes, externally graded exam; small score differences unlikely to reflect large ability gaps.

A2. No precise manipulation of SEA scores around cutoffs.  
     Plausible but testable. Teachers/families cannot observe exact cutoffs ex-ante; scoring is centralized.

A3. Monotonicity: crossing the cutoff weakly raises the probability of attending the higher-quality school for every student.  
     Plausible given the central assignment algorithm.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): one student’s assignment does not directly affect another’s outcomes within the local bandwidth.  
     Reasonable given cohort sizes and large total pool.

A5. Local overlap/common support: students exist on both sides of each cutoff within chosen bandwidths.  
     Satisfied by design; bandwidth can be widened if sample thin.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / sorting around the cutoff  
   • McCrary density test on running variable.  
   • Balance checks for predetermined covariates.  
   • If evidence of bunching, restrict to regions without sorting; use donut RD (drop ±1 point).

T2. Heterogeneous cutoffs, multiple schools  
   • Implement a multi-cutoff FRD with school-by-cohort fixed effects (Lee & Card, 2008 framework).  
   • Allow for school-specific slopes; cluster standard errors at school-cohort level.

T3. Differential attrition / missing outcomes (e.g., migration, drop-out)  
   • Test for continuity of attrition rates at the cutoff.  
   • Use inverse-probability weighting or Lee bounds to gauge robustness.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data manip
library(fixest)          # regression & IV
library(rdrobust)        # FRD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
# ------------------------------------------
# Assume master file: students.csv
dt <- fread("students.csv")

# ------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ------------------------------------------
# Center running variable at each school*year cutoff
dt[, running := SEA_score - school_cutoff]  # cutoff provided in data
# Treatment indicator: attending high-quality school
dt[, treat := as.integer(school_quality == "high")]
# Outcome: standardized Form 3 test z-score
dt[, y := (form3_total - mean(form3_total, na.rm=TRUE))/
           sd(form3_total, na.rm=TRUE)]

# Bandwidth (±20 points default); keep obs within
bw <- 20
dt_rd <- dt[abs(running) <= bw]

# ------------------------------------------
# 3. Main FRD specification (2SLS within fixest)
# ------------------------------------------
# First stage: treat ~ cutoff dummy
dt_rd[, cutoff := as.integer(running >= 0)]

feols_2sls <- feols(y ~ 1 | treat ~ cutoff | 0 |
                    school_id + cohort, data = dt_rd,
                    cluster = ~school_id + cohort)
summary(feols_2sls)

# ------------------------------------------
# 4. rdrobust (non-parametric, local linear)
# ------------------------------------------
frd <- rdrobust(y = dt$y, x = dt$running, c = 0,
                fuzzy = dt$treat)
summary(frd)

# ------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: different bandwidth & donut
# ------------------------------------------
# (a) Narrower bandwidth ±10
dt_rd10 <- dt[abs(running) <= 10]
feols_2sls10 <- update(feols_2sls, data = dt_rd10)
# (b) Donut: drop ±1 point
dt_donut <- dt[abs(running) > 1 & abs(running) <= bw]
feols_donut <- update(feols_2sls, data = dt_donut)
# (c) Covariate balance on gender
balance <- feols(female ~ cutoff + poly(running,2), data = dt_rd)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (peer effects, school resources) predicts positive impacts:

• Short-run academic achievement: +0.10 to +0.20 SD in Form 3 scores.  
• High-stakes exam (CSEC) pass rates: 5–8 p.p. higher.  
• Long-run tertiary enrollment: 5 p.p. increase.  
Magnitude likely attenuates because FRD LATE is measured on marginal admits who may gain less than average top-school students.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (FRD)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No sorting/manipulation of running variable …………… 0.9  
C2: Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff ……………… 0.8  
C3: First-stage relevance (jump in treatment prob) ………… 1.0  
C4: Correct functional form / bandwidth choice …………… 0.8  
C5: External validity beyond local margin …………………… 0.4  

(Overall: strong internal validity; external validity inherently local.)

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
